comment: Stories cut from Homer, Iliad (Butler 1898), Books IV, VIII, XI, XII, XVII, XIX.

region.zh: 特洛伊平原（象徵性定位）

source.work: Homer, Iliad, trans. Samuel Butler (1898), Book XI

summary.en: Zeus, by Iris, tells Hector to hold back while Agamemnon rages. The king charges first, kills Iphidamas — a bridegroom of twelve days — and Coon, and is wounded in the arm by the spear of Coon, Antenor's eldest son. As long as the blood is warm he goes on killing with spear, sword and stone; when the blood dries and the pain comes on him like the pangs of childbirth, he is driven to his chariot, and Hector, freed of his fear, takes the command.
summary.zh: 宙斯遣伊里斯告赫克托耳：阿伽門農逞威時暫避其鋒。王首當其衝，斬伊菲達瑪斯（僅成婚十二日的新郎）與科翁，又被科翁刺傷臂膊。血流溫熱時，他以矛、劍、巨石連連殺敵；血止痛起如產婦陣痛，方被迫登車；赫克托耳如釋重負，遂掌戰局。

sensitivity.note: Ancient literary source; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Zeus sent Iris down to Hector: so long as Agamemnon headed his men and made havoc of the Trojan ranks, Hector was to keep aloof and bid the others bear the brunt; but when the king were wounded by spear or arrow and took to his chariot, then would Zeus vouchsafe him strength to slay till he reached the ships and night fell.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Homer, Iliad, Book 11 (Butler 1898); not verbatim.

passages.text: Iphidamas, son of Antenor, a bridegroom of twelve days, came first against the king: his spear struck the silver-studded girdle below the cuirass and was turned aside as if it had been lead; and Agamemnon caught it from his hand, drew him in with the fury of a lion, and killed him with a sword-cut on the neck. So there the poor fellow lay, 'sleeping a sleep as it were of bronze,' far from his wedded wife, of whom he had had no joy though he had given a hundred cattle and promised a thousand more.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Homer, Iliad, Book 11 (Butler 1898); not verbatim.

passages.text: Coon, Antenor's eldest son, crept up unseen and drove his spear through the king's forearm. Agamemnon was convulsed with pain, but did not leave off fighting: he sprang upon Coon as he dragged the dead body of his brother, and struck him with his bronze-shod spear, killing him over Iphidamas — and then cut off his head. Thus did the sons of Antenor meet their fate at the hands of the son of Atreus, and go down together into the house of Hades.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Homer, Iliad, Book 11 (Butler 1898); not verbatim.

passages.text: As long as the blood welled warm from the wound the king went on attacking the ranks of the enemy with spear and sword and great handfuls of stone; but when the blood dried and the pain came, sharp as the pangs which the Eilithuiae send upon a woman in labour, he sprang into his chariot with a cry to the two Ajaxes to save the host — and rode from the field.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Homer, Iliad, Book 11 (Butler 1898); not verbatim.

title.zh: 布里塞伊斯哭帕特羅克洛斯

region.zh: 特洛伊希臘營地（象徵性定位）

source.work: Homer, Iliad, trans. Samuel Butler (1898), Book XIX

summary.en: Briseis, the war-prize returned to Achilles' tent, sees the mangled body of Patroclus laid out for the rites, and throws herself upon it. She laments: her own husband and three brothers were killed the same day in the sack of her city, and yet it was Patroclus who had comforted her then, promising that Achilles would marry her in Phthia. The women weep around her — in appearance for Patroclus, in truth for their own sorrows. And Achilles, refusing food, sits by the dead man through the night.
summary.zh: 布里塞伊斯——重返阿基琉斯帳中的戰利品——見帕特羅克洛斯殘軀陳列待殮，撲身其上痛哭。她哀悼：她的丈夫與三個兄弟皆在同日喪生，而當時安慰她的正是帕特羅克洛斯，他許諾阿基琉斯將在弗提亞娶她為妻。婦女們繞其哭泣——貌為亡者，實為己悲。阿基琉斯拒食，徹夜守屍。

sensitivity.note: Ancient literary source; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Briseis, fair as Venus, when she saw the mangled body of Patroclus, flung herself upon it and cried aloud, tearing her breast, her neck, and her lovely face with both her hands.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Homer, Iliad, Book 19 (Butler 1898); not verbatim.

passages.text: Beautiful as a goddess she wept and said: 'Patroclus, dearest friend, when I went hence I left you living; I return, O prince, to find you dead; thus do fresh sorrows multiply upon me one after the other. I saw him to whom my father and mother married me cut down before our city, and my three own dear brothers perished with him on the self-same day.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Homer, Iliad, Book 19 (Butler 1898); not verbatim.

passages.text: 'But you, Patroclus, even when Achilles slew my husband and sacked the city of noble Mynes, told me that I was not to weep, for you said you would make Achilles marry me, and take me back with him to Phthia, and we should have a wedding feast among the Myrmidons. You were always kind to me, and I shall never cease to grieve for you.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Homer, Iliad, Book 19 (Butler 1898); not verbatim.

passages.text: She wept as she spoke, and the women joined in her lament-making, as though their tears were for Patroclus, but in truth each was weeping for her own sorrows. Achilles, refusing meat and drink, lay by the dead man all night, and Zeus, looking down in pity, bade Athena drop nectar and ambrosia into his breast so that he might feel no hunger for what he had to do.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Homer, Iliad, Book 19 (Butler 1898); not verbatim.

title.en: The Fight for the Body of Patroclus
title.zh: 爭奪帕特羅克洛斯遺體

region.zh: 特洛伊平原（象徵性定位）

source.work: Homer, Iliad, trans. Samuel Butler (1898), Book XVII

summary.en: Hector has the armour and wants the body; Ajax and Menelaus want it too, and the two hosts surge around it. Hippothous, son of the Pelasgian Lethus, drags it off by the foot — and Ajax strikes him through the helmet, so that the brain oozes through the crest-socket and the body falls. Phorcys, bestriding Hippothous, is next, and is stabbed in the belly so that his entrails pour out. Aeneas and Hector rally the Trojans; Ajax calls for a fighting retreat around the corpse, and the dead man is carried back to the ships under a rain of spears.
summary.zh: 赫克托耳已奪甲而欲奪屍；埃阿斯與墨涅拉俄斯亦力爭。色雷斯人希波托俄斯拖屍欲走，被埃阿斯一矛貫盔、腦漿溢出而亡；跨騎其上的福爾科斯腹中矛而死。埃涅阿斯與赫克托耳重整特洛伊軍勢；兩位埃阿斯呼籲圍屍且戰且退，終在如雨之矛下將遺體護回船陣。

sensitivity.note: Ancient literary source; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: At first the Trojans drove the Achaeans back, and they withdrew from the dead man daunted; the Trojans did not succeed in killing anyone, but they drew the body away. The Achaeans did not lose it long, for Ajax, foremost of the Danaans after Achilles, rallied them like a wild boar at bay on the mountains, and made towards the front through the phalanxes of the Trojans.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Homer, Iliad, Book 17 (Butler 1898); not verbatim.

passages.text: At this moment Hippothous, brave son of the Pelasgian Lethus, in his zeal for Hector and the Trojans, was dragging the body off by the foot through the press of the fight, having bound a strap round the sinews near the ankle. A mischief soon befell him from which none could save him: Ajax, son of Telamon, sprang forward and smote him on his bronze-cheeked helmet. The plumed headpiece broke about the point of the weapon, struck at once by the spear and the strong hand, so that the bloody brain came oozing out through the crest-socket; his strength failed him, and he let Patroclus' foot drop from his hand, as he fell full length dead upon the body.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Homer, Iliad, Book 17 (Butler 1898); not verbatim.

passages.text: Hector took aim at Ajax with a spear; the spear passed on and struck Schedius, son of noble Iphitus, captain of the Phocaeans, under the middle of the collarbone, and his armour rang as he fell. Ajax struck Phorcys, son of Phaenops, in the middle of the belly as he was bestriding Hippothous, and broke the plate of his cuirass; the spear tore out his entrails and he clutched the ground in his palm as he fell.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Homer, Iliad, Book 17 (Butler 1898); not verbatim.

passages.text: The Argives drew off the bodies of Phorcys and Hippothous and stripped them of their armour; and the two Ajaxes, calling the best of the Achaeans about the corpse of Patroclus, faced the Trojan line and fought round the dead man, giving ground slowly and carrying him with them, until, with the body safe between them, they had it once more among the ships.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Homer, Iliad, Book 17 (Butler 1898); not verbatim.

source.work: Homer, Iliad, trans. Samuel Butler (1898), Book VIII

summary.en: Zeus forbids the gods to help either host, on pain of lightning and Tartarus, and announces his scale: he will not stay his hand until Hector reaches the Achaean ships. The gods sit silent; Athena alone, eager to go down, is checked with a threat; and Zeus hangs his golden scales from the sky, weighing the fates of the two armies, till the Trojans' side sinks toward the plain.
summary.zh: 宙斯嚴禁諸神援助兩軍，違者以雷霆與塔耳塔羅斯為罰，並預告其定局：赫克托耳將直逼希臘船陣。諸神默然；唯雅典娜欲下而止於威嚇之下。宙斯自天懸金秤，權衡兩軍之命，特洛伊一側下沉向平原。

sensitivity.note: Ancient literary source; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: When Morning in her robe of saffron began to suffuse light over the earth, Zeus called the gods in council on the topmost crest of Olympus: 'Hear me, gods and goddesses, that I may speak as I am minded. Let none of you, neither goddess nor god, try to cross me, but obey me every one, that I may bring this matter to an end.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Homer, Iliad, Book 8 (Butler 1898); not verbatim.

passages.text: The penalty, he said, would be swift: any god found working apart, on either side, would be hurled into the darkness of Tartarus by his own hand; and, so far from aiding the Greeks, he would go on letting Hector rage till the ships burned and the Greeks had paid for the wrong done to his anger.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Homer, Iliad, Book 8 (Butler 1898); not verbatim.

passages.text: So the gods sat silent in their places. Only Athena rose, because her heart was hot for the Achaeans, and stood before her father; and Zeus, smiling darkly, bade her sit down and not think of opening battle on her own account: the hand that wielded the thunderbolt was stronger than all Olympus. And she went back to her seat in silence, while the rest of the gods stayed where they were.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Homer, Iliad, Book 8 (Butler 1898); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then Zeus took his stand on Ida's highest crest and hung his golden scales from the sky: on one pan the fates of the Trojans, on the other the fates of the Achaeans, and he lifted the balance by the middle. The Achaeans' side sank down toward the plain; the Trojans' rose toward the heaven; and in that balance the day was given, until night should fall, to Hector and the men of Troy.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Homer, Iliad, Book 8 (Butler 1898); not verbatim.

title.en: Nestor's Tent and the Wounded Kings
title.zh: 涅斯托耳的帳篷與受傷的諸王

region.zh: 特洛伊希臘營地（象徵性定位）

source.work: Homer, Iliad, trans. Samuel Butler (1898), Book XI

summary.en: Machaon, wounded by an arrow, is carried out of the fight in Nestor's chariot. In the old man's tent the fair Hecamede mixes the famous cup — Pramnian wine, goat's-milk cheese grated with bronze, white barley-meal — in the two-handled cup with golden doves feeding on every rim, which none but Nestor could lift when full. As they drink, Nestor, wise as ever, tells how his own sons once fought; and Patroclus, sent by Achilles to learn who had been wounded, is moved by the old man's words to go back and beg Achilles for his armour.
summary.zh: 被箭射傷的瑪卡翁由涅斯托耳之車載出戰場。老將帳中，美貌的赫卡墨得調製名酒：普刺姆尼亞酒、青銅擦磨的山羊乳酪、白大麥粉——盛於四耳雙足、每耳有兩隻金鴿啄食之杯，此杯滿時唯涅斯托耳能舉。飲酒間，老人細述往事；帕特羅克洛斯奉阿基琉斯之命來探傷者，聞言動容，遂返營為友求甲。

sensitivity.note: Ancient literary source; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Machaon the physician, wounded by an arrow, was taken out of the fight in Nestor's chariot; and the old man, setting his horses loose to graze, brought him to his tent by the sea, where Eurymedon took the horses from the chariot and they stood in the breeze to dry the sweat from their shirts.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Homer, Iliad, Book 11 (Butler 1898); not verbatim.

passages.text: Fair Hecamede, whom Nestor had had awarded to him from Tenedos when Achilles took it — a daughter of wise Arsinous, given to Nestor because he excelled all of them in counsel — mixed them a mess: a vessel of bronze, an onion for relish, honey and cakes of barley-meal; and in the cup of rare workmanship, studded with bosses of gold, with four handles on each of which two golden doves were feeding, she grated goat's-milk cheese with a bronze grater, threw in a handful of white barley-meal, and poured Pramnian wine. None but Nestor could lift that cup when it was full.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Homer, Iliad, Book 11 (Butler 1898); not verbatim.

passages.text: As they drank, Nestor turned the talk to the fortunes of the war and to the wounded kings, and blamed the army's faltering; and when Patroclus came, standing at the door in Achilles' armour of state, to learn who had been hurt, the old man took him by the words: he told him of the days when the Pylians had fought the Epeans, and begged him to carry to Achilles' ear the plight of the wounded host — for Achilles, he said, might yet save them all.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Homer, Iliad, Book 11 (Butler 1898); not verbatim.

passages.text: And Patroclus went back along the ships, remembering the old man's words, and carrying with him a comrade wounded in the shoulder — Eurypylus — for the old man's speech had lit in him the first spark of the pity that was to cost him his life.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Homer, Iliad, Book 11 (Butler 1898); not verbatim.

region.zh: 特洛伊平原（象徵性定位）

source.work: Homer, Iliad, trans. Samuel Butler (1898), Book IV

summary.en: The truce is sworn, but the gods are not done: Hera and Athena press Zeus to let the Trojans be made the first oath-breakers, and Athena, in the shape of Laodocus, goes down the Trojan ranks to the archer Pandarus with the promise of glory for shooting Menelaus. The arrow flies through belt and cuirass and grazes the flesh, and the wound bleeds like ivory streaked with purple. Agamemnon, his brother's blood on the wound, walks the host in person — praising the willing and shaming the laggards — and war is made again.
summary.zh: 和約既立而神明未息怒：赫拉與雅典娜促宙斯使特洛伊先毁誓；雅典娜化身拉俄多科斯，下至弓手潘達羅斯，許諾榮耀誘其射墨涅拉俄斯。箭穿腰帶與甲冑、擦破皮肉，如象牙染紫。阿伽門農見兄長傷口流血，親巡全軍——褒勇者、譴懦夫——戰火重燃。

sensitivity.note: Ancient literary source; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: The oaths had been sworn, the lambs sacrificed; but Zeus's daughter Athena, eager to see the Trojans made the first to break them, put on the shape of Laodocus, son of Antenor, and walked the ranks till she found Pandarus, son of Lycaon, the bowman of the Aesopus valley.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Homer, Iliad, Book 4 (Butler 1898); not verbatim.

passages.text: 'Brave son of Lycaon,' she said, 'if you dare send an arrow at Menelaus you will win honour and thanks from all the Trojans, and especially from Alexander, who would be the first to requite you handsomely if he could see Menelaus mount his funeral pyre. Take your aim now, and pray to Lycian Apollo, the famous archer, vowing a hecatomb of firstling lambs when you get home.' His fool's heart was persuaded.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Homer, Iliad, Book 4 (Butler 1898); not verbatim.

passages.text: He took out his bow of wild-ibex horn, sixteen palms long, gold-tipped by a worker in horn; he laid the arrow on the string and prayed to Lycian Apollo as he drew, and let fly. But the blessed gods did not forget Menelaus: Athena caught the shaft and turned it — through belt, cuirass and under-belt — till it grazed his skin, and the blood began to run, dark and purple, down his fair thighs like the streak on a piece of Meonian ivory.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Homer, Iliad, Book 4 (Butler 1898); not verbatim.

passages.text: Agamemnon saw the blood and shuddered; but Menelaus, looking at the arrow's barbs, said the wound was light. The king wept and cried aloud to the host that the Trojans had broken the truce; and with the guilt laid openly on the enemy he went through the ranks on foot, cheering the men he found eager and shaming, in terrible words, those he found shirking — that no Achaean might say the king had not set the war in order again.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Homer, Iliad, Book 4 (Butler 1898); not verbatim.

title.en: The Wall That Was Not Blessed

region.zh: 特洛伊希臘營牆（象徵性定位）

source.work: Homer, Iliad, trans. Samuel Butler (1898), Book XII

summary.en: The Achaeans' trench and wall had been built without hecatombs to the gods, and so, the poet tells us, it did not last: after the war, Poseidon and Apollo turned the rivers of Ida on it and washed it into the sea. In its day, however, it stood. Asius, son of Hyrtacus, in his foolhardiness brought his horses to the wall and died there; Sarpedon led the Lycians over the trench on foot, and the Lycians scaled the wall with stones; and Ajax and Teucer held the parapet, shooting and shoving, until the tide of the assault broke and the Lycian captains turned back.
summary.zh: 希臘人的壕溝與城牆未經祭神便建成，故詩人言其不久存：戰後波塞冬與阿波羅引伊達諸河之水將其沖入海中。然而牆在時，阿西俄斯愚勇驅馬直衝而亡；薩爾佩冬徒步率呂基亞人越壕，攀牆投石；埃阿斯與透克羅斯於牆頭堅守，直到呂基亞攻勢潰退。

sensitivity.note: Ancient literary source; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: The Argives and Trojans fought desperately, and the trench and the high wall above it did not keep the Trojans in check longer; for they had built it to protect their ships, and dug the trench all round it, but they had not offered hecatombs to the gods. It had been built without the consent of the immortals, and therefore it did not last.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Homer, Iliad, Book 12 (Butler 1898); not verbatim.

passages.text: The poet stops the tale to tell its end: so long as Hector lived and Achilles nursed his anger, and so long as the city of Priam remained untaken, the great wall stood firm; but when the bravest of either side were gone, and the city was sacked in the tenth year, then Poseidon and Apollo turned on it the streams of all the rivers from Mount Ida — Rhesus, Heptaporus, Caresus, Rhodius, Grenicus, Aesopus and goodly Scamander with Simois — and for nine days Apollo drove the waters against it while Zeus rained, till the wall was washed into the sea and Neptune with his trident threw its beams and stones into the Hellespont, spreading a great beach of sand over the place where it had been.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Homer, Iliad, Book 12 (Butler 1898); not verbatim.

passages.text: While the wall yet stood, the Trojans and their allies followed the counsel of Polydamas, dismounting and coming over the trench on foot in five companies; but Asius, son of Hyrtacus, in his foolhardiness took his horses and his esquire with him toward the ships, nor did he fail to come by his end in consequence: death of ill-omened name overshadowed him ere he could return to wind-beaten Ilius exulting in his chariot.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Homer, Iliad, Book 12 (Butler 1898); not verbatim.

passages.text: Sarpedon led the Lycians over on foot, with Glaucus and Asteropaeus, and charged straight at the Danaans, holding his shield before him in the manner of a lion. And over the trench and up the wall the Lycians swarmed with stones, while on the parapet stood Ajax and Teucer, Ajax shoving down with great stones what came near, Teucer bending his bow and shooting; and when a Lycian came over the battlement, Ajax took him by the breastplate and cast him out; so the wall held for that day, and the Lycian captains, beaten back, turned again to their ships.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Homer, Iliad, Book 12 (Butler 1898); not verbatim.

region.zh: 伊薩卡與美塞尼（象徵性定位）

source.work: Homer, Odyssey, trans. Samuel Butler (1898), Book XX

summary.en: Athena puts it into Penelope's mind to bring out the great bow; and the poet tells how Odysseus came by it. The bow had been left him by Iphitus, son of Eurytus, whom he met in Messene on a mission to recover sheep stolen from Ithaca; Iphitus had been hunting twelve lost brood mares when he fell in with Heracles — and Heracles, to his shame, killed his guest, fearing neither heaven nor the table he had set before Iphitus, and kept the mares. Iphitus had given Ulysses the bow that mighty Eurytus had carried, and Ulysses had given him a sword and a spear in return — a friendship that, for Heracles' crime, never got to be a visit.
summary.zh: 雅典娜令珀涅羅珀取出大弓；詩人敘其來歷：奧德修斯赴美塞尼追討失羊，途中遇伊菲特斯（歐律托斯之子）——後者為尋十二匹失馬而遇赫拉克勒斯，卻被其殺害，蓋神懼天譴、亦不敬所設之宴。伊菲特斯生前以父之強弓贈奧德修斯，奧德修斯回贈劍矛；友誼未及深交便為赫拉克勒斯之罪所斷。

sensitivity.note: Ancient literary source; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Minerva now put it in Penelope's mind to make the suitors try their skill with the bow and with the iron axes, in contest among themselves, as a means of bringing about their destruction. She went upstairs and got the store-room key, which was made of bronze and had a handle of ivory, and went with her maidens into the store-room at the end of the house, where her husband's treasures were kept — and where was also his bow, and the quiver full of deadly arrows that had been given him by a friend whom he had met in Lacedaemon: Iphitus, son of Eurytus.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Homer, Odyssey, Book 20 (Butler 1898); not verbatim.

passages.text: The two fell in with one another in Messene, at the house of Ortilochus, where Ulysses was staying in order to recover a debt owing from the whole people — for the Messenians had carried off three hundred sheep from Ithaca, and had sailed away with them and with their shepherds. In quest of these Ulysses took a long journey while still quite young, for his father and the other chieftains had sent him on a mission to recover them.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Homer, Odyssey, Book 20 (Butler 1898); not verbatim.

passages.text: Iphitus had gone there also, to try to get back twelve brood mares that he had lost, with the mule foals that were running with them. These mares were the death of him in the end: for when he went to the house of Jove's son, mighty Heracles, who performed such prodigies of valour, Heracles, to his shame, killed him — though he was his guest, for he feared not heaven's vengeance, nor yet respected his own table which he had set before Iphitus, but killed him in spite of everything, and kept the mares himself.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Homer, Odyssey, Book 20 (Butler 1898); not verbatim.

passages.text: It was when claiming these that Iphitus met Ulysses, and gave him the bow which mighty Eurytus had been used to carry, and which, on his death, had been left to his son. Ulysses gave him in return a sword and a spear; and this was the beginning of a fast friendship, though they never visited at one another's houses, for Jove's son Heracles killed Iphitus before they could do so. And when Ulysses sailed for Troy the bow was left behind, a keepsake from a valued friend.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Homer, Odyssey, Book 20 (Butler 1898); not verbatim.

region.zh: 伊薩卡奧德修斯王宮（象徵性定位）

source.work: Homer, Odyssey, trans. Samuel Butler (1898), Books XVII-XVIII

summary.en: Odysseus, in the disguise of a beggar, comes into his own hall with the swineherd, and the humiliation begins: Antinous throws a footstool at him and the household laughs; Melanthius the goatherd rails; and Irus, the town's other beggar — a hulking glutton called Arnaeus, named Irus for running errands — is set on by the suitors to fight him for the doorway. Athena thickens the limbs of the old man; Irus, once sobered by the sight, is beaten almost to death, and dragged out by the heels to be food for dogs and swine.
summary.zh: 偽裝乞丐的奧德修斯隨牧豬人步入自家大廳，羞辱隨之而來：安提諾俄斯擲凳、僕人訕笑、牧羊人墨蘭提俄斯斥罵；城中另一乞丐伊魯斯——本名阿耳奈俄斯、因跑腿而得名的貪食大漢——被求婚者慫恿，為爭門口而與「老乞」較量。雅典娜使老人的肢體粗壯；伊魯斯見狀膽怯仍戰，被幾近打死，拖足拖出，欲作狗豬之食。

sensitivity.note: Ancient literary source; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: There came a certain common tramp who used to go begging all over the city of Ithaca, and was notorious as an incorrigible glutton and drunkard — a great hulking fellow to look at, though he had no strength nor stay in him; his real name, the one his mother gave him, was Arnaeus, but the young men of the place called him Irus, because he used to run errands for anyone who would send him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Homer, Odyssey, Book 18 (Butler 1898); not verbatim.

passages.text: As soon as he came he began to insult Ulysses, and to try to drive him out of his own house: 'Be off, old man, from the doorway, or you shall be dragged out neck and heels. Do you not see that they are all giving me the wink, and wanting me to turn you out by force?' Ulysses frowned and said there was room enough in the doorway for the pair of them; but Irus would not hear it, and Antinous, pleased at the quarrel, offered the victorious beggar sausages and a seat at the suitors' feast if he would clear the hall of the other.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Homer, Odyssey, Book 18 (Butler 1898); not verbatim.

passages.text: Athena stood by the true beggar and thickened his limbs, and when Irus saw the great size of the man's thighs he came near fainting; but the suitors had given their word, and the fight was fought in the hall for the prize of the puddings. Ulysses, mindful of his own plan, did not quite kill him: he broke him about the jaw, and he fell in the doorway with a thud, and the household laughed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Homer, Odyssey, Book 18 (Butler 1898); not verbatim.

passages.text: And Eurymachus, in his mockery, hurled a footstool at the old man; the stool hit the cupbearer on his right hand and knocked him down, and his wine-jug rang to the ground. The suitors, in an uproar, wished the stranger gone — 'we cannot permit such disturbance about a beggar' — and Ulysses, nursing his anger, went out and sat among the swineherd and the cattle, saying to himself what he would do to the whole of them before the day was out.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Homer, Odyssey, Books 17-18 (Butler 1898); not verbatim.
